When you desperately want something, work toward it, or try very hard to make it happen — and then something or someone completely stops you from getting there — you are thwarted. The word describes the state of being blocked, stopped, or defeated in your effort or desire before it could succeed.

Think of it this way: a river flowing powerfully forward hits a dam and is stopped dead. That river is thwarted. Its force, its direction, its intention — all of it was there, and all of it was stopped.

The adjective can describe two things:

1. A person — someone whose desire, goal, or attempt was prevented from succeeding.

A thwarted lover stands outside the door, unable to reach the person he loves.
The thwarted criminal was arrested before he could rob the bank.

2. A plan, attempt, ambition, or desire — something that was stopped before it could be carried out or fulfilled.

The thwarted escape plan left the prisoners with no hope.
Her thwarted ambitions left a wound that never fully healed.
A thwarted attempt to seize power ended his political career.

Here's what makes "thwarted" richer than a plain word like "stopped" or "blocked."

When something is thwarted, there is almost always an emotional charge attached to it — a sense of frustration, bitterness, or deep disappointment. The word quietly tells you that the person wanted this badly, tried hard, and was then cut off. It carries the weight of that failure.

If I say "his plan was stopped," it's just a fact. If I say "his plan was thwarted," you feel the sting of it — the effort that went nowhere, the goal that was snatched away.

This is why "thwarted" appears so often alongside emotionally heavy words:

  • thwarted ambitions (dreams that were crushed)
  • thwarted desires (deep wants that were never met)
  • thwarted love (romantic pursuit that was blocked or rejected)
  • thwarted villain (someone whose scheme was defeated — often with a sense of drama)

"Thwarted" means the blocking was complete, not partial. It doesn't mean "slightly slowed down" or "made more difficult." It means the effort was stopped in its tracks — the goal was not reached.

A person can be repeatedly thwarted — blocked again and again each time they try — which often builds a deep sense of helplessness or resentment.

Every time she tried to speak up, she was thwarted by those in power.
Nuances That Set It Apart from Similar Words

Thwarted vs. Frustrated:
Both carry a sense of being blocked and emotionally affected. But "frustrated" is more about the internal feeling, while "thwarted" is more about the external blocking — something actively stopped you. You feel frustrated; you are thwarted.

Thwarted vs. Foiled:
Very close in meaning. "Foiled" is often used in slightly dramatic or literary contexts (think comic books: "foiled again!"). "Thwarted" is more natural in everyday serious writing and covers a wider range — it can describe ambitions and emotions, not just schemes and plans.

Thwarted vs. Blocked:
"Blocked" is neutral — a road can be blocked; a drain can be blocked. It carries no emotional weight. "Thwarted" is specifically about effort, desire, or intent being stopped, and it always implies something was at stake for the person involved.

Thwarted vs. Stymied:
"Stymied" means you're stuck and don't know how to move forward — like being baffled. "Thwarted" means something or someone actively stopped you. The source of the problem is different.

These are the most natural combinations you'll encounter or use:

  • thwarted ambitions — life goals that were prevented from being achieved
  • thwarted plans — schemes or arrangements that were stopped before they could be carried out
  • thwarted attempt — an effort that was blocked and did not succeed
  • thwarted desires — wants or cravings that were denied or prevented
  • thwarted efforts — repeated trying that kept being stopped
  • feel thwarted — to feel as though something is constantly blocking you
  • thwarted by circumstances — stopped not by a person but by the situation itself
A Few Sentences to See It in Action

• The thwarted general retreated into bitterness after his campaign was stopped by his own government.
  • Her thwarted desire to study medicine haunted her for the rest of her life.
  • He felt thwarted at every turn — no matter what he tried, something always stood in the way.
  • The detective's investigation, thwarted by lack of evidence, eventually came to a dead end.
  • A thwarted plan to renovate the house left the family living in chaos for months.

Thwarted describes the state of being completely stopped or blocked from achieving what you were trying to do or deeply wanted. It applies to both people (a thwarted artist) and their plans, ambitions, attempts, or desires (thwarted ambitions). Unlike neutral words such as "blocked," "thwarted" carries emotional weight — a quiet sense of frustration, bitterness, or defeat. The blocking is total, not partial, and the word always implies that effort or desire was present before the stopping occurred. It is one of those words that captures not just what happened, but how it felt.
